claims.claim: Hobb says she writes a great deal in first person because she regards it as the natural storytelling voice, likening it to a person recounting their day at home.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: first person is the natural storytelling voice
claims.page: first half, 'I write… a tremendous amount of my work is first person'

claims.claim: Hobb says what a first-person narrator notices on entering a room is determined by who he is, contrasting an assassin entering a room with three people in it against a child looking for a lost toy.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: what he notices is going to be very different
claims.page: second half, 'If you’re writing from the first person'

claims.claim: Hobb derives a character's personality from household economy, explaining a pennypinching character by a childhood family on a very tight budget in which every choice was consequential.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: Charlotte grew up in a family with a very tight budget
claims.page: first half, 'Why is she so pennypinching?'

claims.claim: Hobb says that for her the character has to be generated by the world, and that she could not believably insert a twenty-first century person into a fantasy.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: the character has to be generated by the world
claims.page: first half, answer to the opening question

claims.feature: other: reaction to a minor character as characterisation
claims.claim: Hobb offers an inn scene as a characterisation test: a late serving boy, and whether the viewpoint character fails to notice, is annoyed at someone else's shouting, is embarrassed, or quietly tips the boy.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: whether you quietly tip the kid
claims.page: second half, 'How a character treats a secondary character'

claims.claim: The essayist argues Hobb's method is to place the reader inside Fitz's perspective and leave them there, supplying no outside witness to frame him.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: Hobb places you inside Fitz’s perspective and leaves you there

claims.claim: The essayist argues that Fitz's competence is legible only by inference because he almost never narrates his own power, reporting instead his doubts, failures, grief and shame.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: he almost never narrates his own power

claims.claim: The essayist shows Hobb rendering a character's training as an inventory of ordinary objects in a room, listing medicinal unguents on the mantel, two pens at the ready and a Stones puzzle on the table.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: the medicinal unguents on the mantel, the two pens

claims.claim: The essayist argues that Fitz-as-chronicler records what official chroniclers could not, and that history in Hobb is made in bedrooms, kitchens, stables and sickrooms as well as in councils and battles.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: history is not made only in councils and battles
claims.page: section 'A Writer, Historian, and Chronicler of His Age'

claims.claim: The essayist warns that the intimacy of Fitz's prose should not be mistaken for simplicity, crediting it with clear rendering of character, politics, landscape, memory and moral conflict.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: intimacy should not be mistaken for simplicity
claims.page: section 'A Writer, Historian, and Chronicler of His Age'

claims.claim: The essayist says Hobb hides her protagonist's magnificence in plain sight, leaving it to the reader whether to see past his harsh self-assessment.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: She hides his magnificence in plain sight

claims.claim: Hobb, quoted by the reporter, says she tries to express how horrifying and ugly violence is, and says depictions that make violence beautiful or satisfying make her uncomfortable as a reader.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, quoted by Pauline Bock, New Statesman, 27 July 2018 (interviewed at Imaginales, May 2018)
claims.quote: I try to express how horrifying and ugly violence is

claims.claim: The reporter observes that in Hobb's world names can embody a character's virtues, listing the brothers Chivalry, Nimble, Swift, Steady, Just and Hearth.
claims.source: Pauline Bock (reporter's paraphrase), New Statesman, 27 July 2018
claims.quote: names can embody a character’s virtues
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'In Hobb’s Elderlings universe, names matter'

claims.claim: The reporter describes the captain Kyle Haven as a name that reflects poorly on its bearer, whose greed creates endless trouble for his ship and his family's business.
claims.source: Pauline Bock (reporter's paraphrase), New Statesman, 27 July 2018
claims.quote: whose greediness creates endless troubles for his ship and family’s business
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'In Hobb’s Elderlings universe, names matter'

claims.claim: The reporter characterises the Elderlings societies by their institutions in a single clause each, calling Bingtown matriarchal and business-oriented against the macho warring state of Chalced.
claims.source: Pauline Bock (reporter's paraphrase), New Statesman, 27 July 2018
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Her books tell tales of dragons and pirates'
